newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - As Iraqi supply looms, winter rescues OPEC.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - As Iraqi supply looms, winter rescues OPEC.

text.p: A revived prospect that Iraq may soon sell oil again has highlighted the failure of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries to act as a true commodity cartel.

Western monitors calculate that rampant violations of their mandated output quotas by others in OPEC, which meets in Vienna this week, already exceed a volume that it has pencilled in for Iraq by almost a million barrels a day.

Oil ministers gathering on Tuesday for their twice-yearly conference on production levels put a brave face on news from New York that a deal to relax the U.N. Gulf War ban on Iraqi oil exports may finally be ready to implement.
"There will be no impact whatsoever," said Nigeria's Dan Etete, when reporters asked what he thought the extra barrels would do to prices.
"It is not a surprise...they can come back today and it would make no difference".
Analysts agree that the market is unlikely to collapse, citing frantic demand to fill depleted Western stocks of heating fuel. Winter snow greeted OPEC in Vienna on Tuesday.
But the analysts predict that resumed Iraqi sales plus OPEC quota violations may mean some erosion of prices in 1997.
"The market is tight and it can take anything that is thrown at it right now", said Geoff Pyne, an energy eocnomist with UBS Limited in London.
"But if Iraq returns soon it could be that prices will soften more quickly in the spring than we had expected".
With Iraq selling again, Pyne predicts an average 1997 price for the benchmark Brent Blend of North Sea crude at around $18.50 per barrel compared with $20 so far this year.

Allowing for inflation, a barrel at $18.50 is modestly better - by about $3.50 in today's money - than the price back in 1973 when an Arab oil embargo on the West gave OPEC a chance to assert itself as a cartel.

But it compares with OPEC's own declared target of $21 for a basket of world crude oils - equating to about $22 for Brent - set as long ago as 1990 just before Iraq invaded fellow founder member Kuwait and provoked the U.N. ban on its oil.

A committee of the ministers of Iran, Nigeria and Libya met in Vienna on Tuesday with OPEC secretary-general Rilwanu Lukman of Nigeria to review the vexed issue of quota compliance ahead of full ministerial talks on Wednesday.
Western industry monitors say the arithmetic is depressing as a measure of the efficiency of the once-mighty cartel.
Current quotas, likely to be kept unchanged until mid-1997, add up to a ceiling on total volume at 25.03 million barrels daily.
That includes an extra allocation pencilled in in June for the Iraqi exports that have yet to begin. But actual OPEC supply, monitors say, is already almost 26 million.
One of the 11 members, Venezuela, is alone alleged to be in excess by about 800,000 barrels - equal to the extra assigned for Iraq.
Monitors say that only OPEC linchpin Saudi Arabia, with 2.0 million barrels of its capacity in mothballs, and Gulf allies Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates, are holding back considerable volumes.
They are in effect acting by themselves in the role of world "swing" producer that OPEC once aspired to.
